fields.title: Crise Humanitaire Complexe et Épidémies - République démocratique du Congo : Rapport de Situation Semaine No 41 (5 au 11 octobre 2026)
fields.body:
**Résumé de la situation épidémiologique et humanitaire**

Situation épidémiologique

▪ Épidémie de MVE : Depuis le début de l’épidémie jusqu’au 24 octobre 2026, 9 964 cas confirmés dont 4 841 décès (létalité : 48,6 %) ont été enregistrés avec 66 ZS touchées à travers 8 provinces (Haut-Uélé, Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé, Sud-Ubangi et Nord-Ubangi). Par ailleurs, 2 670 personnes ont été déclarées guéries. Au cours des dernières 24 heures, 88 nouveaux cas confirmés dont 38 décès (26 décès communautaires et 12 intra-CTE) ont été notifiés dans les provinces de l’Ituri (44 cas), du Nord-Kivu (39 cas) et Haut-Uélé (5 cas).

▪ Épidémie de choléra : Un total de 58 312 cas suspects et 1 715 décès (létalité : 2,9 %) a été rapporté depuis le début de l’année jusqu’à la S41/2026 dans 243 ZS réparties dans 20 provinces, tandis qu’à une période similaire de l’année 2025, 58 571 cas suspects et 1 783 décès (létalité : 3,0 %) étaient notifiés dans 234 ZS appartenant à 20 provinces.  
On observe une baisse de 35,6 % au terme de la S41/2026 (données incomplètes) où 1 686 cas suspects et 57 décès (létalité : 3,4 %) ont été notifiés dans 93 ZS à travers 18 provinces comparativement à la S40/2026, au cours de laquelle, 2 617 cas et 95 décès (létalité : 3,6 %) avaient été enregistrés dans 100 ZS de 17 provinces. La province du Haut-Katanga vient en tête de notification avec un cumul hebdomadaire de 361 cas suspects.

▪ Épidémie de mpox : Au terme de la S41/2026, 587 cas suspects et 9 décès (létalité : 1,5 %) sont notifiés dans 79 ZS de 17 provinces contre 690 cas et 9 décès (létalité : 1,3 %) rapportés dans 84 ZS de 19 provinces, soit une baisse de 14,9 % observée entre les deux semaines. Depuis le début de l’année jusqu’à la S41/2026, 33 371 cas suspects de mpox et 367 décès (létalité 1,1 %) ont été rapportés dans 365 ZS réparties dans les 26 provinces comparativement à 79 936 cas suspects et 763 décès (létalité : 1,0 %) qui étaient notifiés dans 448 ZS de 26 provinces au cours de la même période de l’année précédente, exprimant une baisse de 58,3 % des cas entre les deux années. ▪ Épidémie de rougeole : À travers 72 ZS appartenant à 20 provinces, 385 cas suspects et 4 décès (létalité : 1,0 %) ont été notifiés à l’issue de la S41/2026 contre 658 cas suspects et 9 décès (létalité : 1,4 %) rapportés dans 108 ZS de 22 provinces. Entre la S1 et S41/2026, 129 145 cas et 1 690 décès (létalité : 1,3 %) ont été notifiés dans 495 (95,4 %) ZS de 26 provinces, suggérant 106,8 % de hausse comparativement à 62 455 cas et 925 décès (létalité : 1,5 %) enregistrés dans 469 (90,4 %) ZS réparties dans toutes les provinces du pays, à une période similaire de l’année 2025.

▪ Situation humanitaire (province du Sud-Kivu)

Environ 22 500 personnes (3 750 ménages) déplacées à la suite des affrontements armés dans les hauts plateaux d’Uvira. Le 10 octobre 2026, de nouveaux mouvements de populations ont été signalés dans les hauts plateaux d’Uvira et d’Itombwe, à la suite d’affrontements armés. Ces nouvelles vagues ont fui les villages de Magunda, Binjigi, Nyongombero et Musondjon en groupement de Basimukinje II, en secteur d’Itombwe (Mwenga), pour trouver refuge dans les localités environnantes. Les personnes déplacées se sont principalement installées dans les aires de santé de Maheta, Magunda, Rubemba, dans le territoire d’Uvira.

fields.title: Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: In Niania, dialogue transforms mistrust into community engagement
fields.body:
**Niania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo—** Reverend Bienvenu Ndombe never imagined that one day he would encourage his congregation to trust the teams responding to the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus. At the start of the outbreak, this representative of revival churches in the Bandaka chiefdom was himself plagued by doubts.

In his community, rumours claimed that health teams were using substances to contaminate toilets and shower areas. Others alleged that patients taken to the Ebola treatment centre (ETC) never returned alive. “When I heard all these rumours myself, it was difficult to know what to believe because so many people were talking about them. We thought it might be a commercial scheme linked to Ebola,” he recalls.

His perception changed when he took part in a community dialogue with response teams. Together with other religious leaders, he later visited the Niania Ebola treatment centre to see first-hand how patients were being cared for.  
“We spoke with patients. We saw that they were receiving proper care, recovering and returning home,” he says. Since then, Reverend Bienvenu has encouraged his congregation to seek care at the ETC promptly if they develop symptoms.

In the Babonde area Sébastien Mugiamaro, a school administrator, was also deeply affected by the outbreak. When he fell ill, Sébastien sought medical attention immediately. Tests ruled out Ebola and enabled him to receive appropriate treatment.

“I lost my mother, then my father, to Ebola. When I started experiencing severe headaches, I immediately thought about the disease. I knew that early treatment could give me a chance of recovery,” he explains. This is the same message he shares within his community. “I urge residents to seek medical care as soon as symptoms appear rather than relying on rumours,” he says.

Misinformation about seeking care and accepting health interventions can have serious consequences, including preventable deaths. To address this, the Ministry of Public Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners, has strengthened risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) activities. These efforts help communities better understand how to protect themselves and what actions to take when the first signs of the disease appear.

“When rumours emerge, our priority is to listen to community concerns and provide concrete responses,” explains Dr Joseph Pemanakue Babundiak, Chief Medical Officer of Niania Health Zone. “Dialogue allows us to gradually rebuild trust, encourage early care-seeking and strengthen community participation in the Ebola response.”

Paulin Koingo, a community mobilizer, notes that concerns raised by residents have helped shape response strategies. Community dialogues were organized with traditional leaders, religious leaders, young people, women’s associations, motorcycle taxi drivers and traditional healers. These discussions were accompanied by practical demonstrations on safe and dignified burials and on preparing chlorinated solutions for infection prevention and control.

On 11 August 2026, a community dialogue in Likpangola brought together around 55 participants, and 52 stated that they wished to contribute to the response. On 10 September, an awareness campaign reached nearly 2500 people in the Juhudi and Bafwabango health areas. Two days later, 110 community volunteers, including 45 women, took part in an orientation session. Radio spots in French, Swahili and Lingala, together with several radio programmes, were also broadcast on five community radio stations.

These initiatives have helped facilitate interventions that were previously contested, particularly safe burials, decontamination activities and the referral of suspected cases to health facilities.

For Dr Bavon Tangunza Ngunga, who oversees infodemic management and RCCE at the WHO office in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, responding to rumours involves more than simply disseminating messages. “A rumour cannot be resolved by a message alone. It may reflect fear, a negative healthcare experience or a practical need, such as rapid access to a treatment centre,” he explains.

WHO is therefore supporting health authorities to analyse concerns raised by communities, conduct targeted social listening sessions with leaders of different groups and adjust interventions accordingly.

Some concerns nevertheless persist, highlighting the need to continue dialogue and promote early care-seeking.

Reverend Bienvenu reflects on the progress achieved. “Today, we have confidence. We tell the population to trust the response teams because the disease is real. People are now beginning to understand and participate more actively in the fight against the virus affecting them,” he concludes.

fields.title: Bulletin trimestriel du Consortium SAFER, Édition N°2 | Juillet - Septembre 2026
fields.body:
**EDITO**

La détérioration du contexte humanitaire s’est poursuivie au cours du trimestre, marquée à la fois par une augmentation des mouvements de population et par l’expansion de l’épidémie d’Ebola. Selon les données de suivi des alertes, 78 déplacements ont été enregistrés dans 25 territoires, affectant près de 277 461 ménages (Source : EHtools/analyse et visualisation CAT-DRC). Dans le même temps, l’épidémie d’Ebola a touché sept provinces et 63 zones de santé, avec 8 300 cas et 4 018 décès rapportés (source : SitRep No139/MBE-BDB/30/09/2026). Ces dynamiques ont entraîné une hausse des besoins humanitaires, nécessitant le maintien d’une capacité de réponse rapide et adaptée aux populations les plus vulnérables.

Malgré ce contexte, SAFER a poursuivi sa réponse d’urgence auprès des communautés affectées tout en renforçant son plaidoyer auprès des bailleurs. Ces efforts ont contribué à l’obtention de financements de 10 M USD du FH RDC et de 5 M GBP du FCDO, ainsi qu’à des échanges stratégiques avec ECHO à Bruxelles. En septembre, SAFER a également lancé deux interventions pilotes de mobile money, élargissant ainsi ses modalités d’assistance et sa capacité d’adaptation aux réalités du terrain

fields.title: SAFER Consortium Quarterly Bulletin, Issue No. 2 | July - September 2026
fields.body:
**EDITORIAL**

The humanitarian context continued to deteriorate during the quarter, marked by both an increase in population movements and the expansion of the Ebola outbreak. According to alert monitoring data, 78 displacement incidents were recorded across 25 territories, affecting nearly 277,461 households (Source: EHtools/CAT-DRC analysis and visualization). At the same time, the Ebola outbreak affected seven provinces and 63 Health Zones, with 8,300 cases and 4,018 reported deaths (Source: SitRep No. 139/MBE-BDB/30/09/2026). These developments led to rising humanitarian needs, requiring the sustained capacity to provide rapid and appropriate assistance to the most vulnerable populations. Despite this challenging context, SAFER continued its emergency response to affected communities while strengthening its advocacy efforts with donors. These efforts contributed to securing USD 10 million from the DRC Humanitarian Fund (FH RDC) and GBP 5 million from the FCDO, as well as enabling strategic engagements with ECHO in Brussels.

In September, SAFER also launched two pilot mobile money interventions, thereby expanding its assistance modalities and enhancing its ability to adapt to field realities.

fields.title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 91, as of 27 October 2026
fields.body:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- Women living with obstetric fistula receive medical treatment in Haute-Kotto.
- High cross-border population mobility between the DRC and south-eastern CAR continues to pose a significant risk of Ebola virus disease (EVD) cross-border transmission.
- More than 1,500 people undertake preventive displacement in Ouham-Pendé.

**GENERAL CONTEXT**

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Central Region

- On 21 October, a staff member from a humanitarian organization was threatened by armed elements. Community members and staff from a United Nations agency were also subjected to similar threats. One day earlier, another NGO staff member received verbal threats from an armed individual while carrying out child protection activities. These incidents highlight an operating environment marked by increasing risks for humanitarian actors and the populations they assist.

Ouham-Pendé Prefecture – Western Region

- Approximately 1,500 people pre-emptively fled Bilsem village on 21 October due to security concerns. Displaced households sought refuge in the bush, at temporary farming sites, or in nearby localities, including Gaïboula, located 5 km from Bocaranga. The population movement followed community tensions arising from a dispute between a herder and a farmer. The following day, local authorities intervened to ease tensions and strengthen security measures. Following improvements in the security situation, the displaced people returned to their areas of origin.

**HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE**

**Health**

Countrywide

- As of the reporting, no Ebola cases have been recorded in the Central African Republic (CAR). According to a regional analysis by REACH, the Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to expand across the northeastern provinces, with 9,637 confirmed cases and 4,602 deaths reported as of 18 October 2026. The outbreak has recently spread to the health zones of Dungu, Alimbongo, Ango and Wapinda, the latter two, located in close proximity to the CAR border. Population mobility data indicate that population movements and economic exchanges along major road and river corridors could facilitate cross-border transmission, particularly between Nord-Ubangi and the Central African prefectures of Basse-Kotto and Haut-Mbomou. The localities of Yakoma, Gbadolite (DRC, bordering south-eastern CAR) and Zemio have been identified as particularly exposed to risks associated with cross-border movements. Furthermore, the presence of more than 264,000 Central African refugees and asylum seekers in the DRC, mainly in Nord-Ubangi, Sud-Ubangi and Bas-Uele provinces, could increase cross-border movements between the two countries and heighten the risk of virus importation. In this context, enhanced epidemiological surveillance at points of entry, early detection of suspected cases, and preparedness of health facilities in border areas remain critical to mitigating the risk of disease spread in the Central African Republic. In August, the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$3 million to strengthen prevention efforts in high-risk areas, reinforce surveillance and isolation capacities, support community engagement, and improve access to water.

**Protection**

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

- On the margins of the high-level visit to Zemio on 21 October by the Prime Minister of the Central African Republic, accompanied by several government ministers, the Humanitarian Coordinator and representatives of United Nations agencies, UNFPA distributed dignity kits to 50 survivors of gender-based violence (GBV). The kits included bags, cloth wraps, towels, sanitary pads, toothpaste, toothbrushes, laundry and bathing soap, underwear and body cream.

fields.title: République centrafricaine : Rapport de situation N° 91 (au 27 octobre 2026)
fields.body:
**FAITS SAILLANTS**

- Des femmes souffrant de fistules obstétricales reçoivent une prise en charge médicale dans la Haute-Kotto.
- La mobilité transfrontalière entre la RDC et le Sud-Est de la RCA maintient un risque élevé de propagation de la maladie à virus Ebola.
- Plus de 1500 personnes se déplacent préventivement dans l’Ouham-Péndé.

**CONTEXTE GÉNÉRAL**

Préfecture de la Haute-Kotto – Centre

- Le 21 octobre, un membre du personnel d’une organisation humanitaire a fait l’objet de menaces de la part d’éléments armés. Des membres de la communauté ainsi que du personnel d’une agence des Nations Unies ont également été concernés par des menaces similaires. Un jour plus tôt, un autre membre du personnel d’une ONG a également fait l’objet de menaces verbales proférées par un individu armé alors qu’il menait des activités de protection de l’enfance. Ces incidents illustrent un environnement opérationnel marqué par des risques croissants pour les acteurs humanitaires et les populations qu’ils assistent.

Préfecture de l’Ouham-Péndé – Ouest

- Environ 1 500 personnes ont quitté préventivement le village de Bilsem le 21 octobre, en raison de préoccupations liées à la sécurité. Les ménages déplacés se sont réfugiés dans la brousse, dans des campements champêtres ou dans des localités voisines, notamment à Gaïboula, située à 5 km de Bocaranga. Ce mouvement de population fait suite à des tensions communautaires consécutives à un différend entre un éleveur et un agriculteur. Un jour plus tard, les autorités locales sont intervenues pour apaiser les tensions et renforcer les mesures de sécurité. Les personnes qui se sont déplacées ont regagné leur domicile après une accalmie.

**BESOINS ET RÉPONSE HUMANITAIRE**

**Santé**

Au niveau national

- À ce jour, aucun cas d’Ebola n’a été enregistré en RCA. Selon une analyse régionale de l’ONG REACH, la flambée de maladie à virus Ebola en République démocratique du Congo (RDC) continue de s'étendre dans les provinces du nord-est, avec 9 637 cas confirmés et 4 602 décès recensés au 18 octobre 2026. L'épidémie a récemment atteint les zones de santé de Dungu, Alimbongo, Ango et Wapinda, les deux dernières étant situées à proximité immédiate de la frontière avec la RCA. Les données de mobilité indiquent que les mouvements de populations et les échanges économiques le long des principaux axes routiers et fluviaux pourraient favoriser une transmission transfrontalière, notamment entre le Nord-Ubangi et les préfectures centrafricaines de Basse-Kotto et du Haut-Mbomou. Les localités de Yakoma, Gbadolite (RDC, à la frontière avec le sud-est de la RCA) et Zémio sont identifiées comme particulièrement exposées aux risques liés aux déplacements transfrontaliers. Par ailleurs, la présence de plus de 264 000 réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile centrafricains en RDC, principalement dans les provinces du Nord-Ubangi, du Sud-Ubangi et du Bas-Uele, pourrait accroître les mouvements pendulaires entre les deux pays et augmenter le risque d'importation du virus. Dans ce contexte, le maintien d'une surveillance épidémiologique renforcée aux points d'entrée, la détection précoce des cas suspects et la préparation des structures sanitaires dans les zones frontalières demeurent essentiels pour limiter le risque de propagation de la maladie en République centrafricaine. Le Fonds central pour les interventions d’urgence (CERF) a alloué en août dernier 3 millions de dollars américains pour renforcer les efforts de prévention dans les régions à risque, renforcer la surveillance, les capacités d’isolation, l’engagement communautaire et l’accès à l’eau.

**Protection**

Préfecture du Haut-Mbomou – Sud-Est

- En marge de la visite de haut niveau effectuée à Zémio par le Premier ministre de la RCA en compagnie de certains ministres, du Coordonnateur Humanitaire et des Chefs d’agences des Nations Unies le 21 octobre, UNFPA a distribué des kits de dignité comprenant des sacs, des pagnes, serviettes, garniture, pâte dentifrice, brosse à dent, savons à linge et à toilette, sous-vêtement et crème à 50 survivantes de violences basées sur le genre (VBG) à Zémio.

fields.title: Nord-Kivu : de nouvelles équipes d’intervention rapide se préparent à renforcer la riposte contre la maladie à virus Bundibugyo
fields.body:
**Beni, République démocratique du Congo, 28 octobre 2026** - Sous les arbres et dans l’atmosphère studieuse d’un espace de formation en plein air à Beni, 48 professionnels de santé viennent de franchir une étape décisive. Pendant trois jours, épidémiologistes, cliniciens, infirmiers, spécialistes de la prévention et logisticiens ont travaillé côte à côte pour se préparer à une même mission : intervenir rapidement et efficacement face à la maladie à virus Bundibugyo.

À l'issue de cette formation intensive, deux nouvelles équipes d’intervention rapide (EIR) ont été constituées. Prêtes à être déployées selon les besoins, elles viendront booster les capacités opérationnelles de la réponse dans les zones les plus affectées et reculées du Nord-Kivu, tout en permettant le maintien des services de santé essentiels.

Le dernier jour, un exercice de simulation grandeur nature plonge les participant(e)s dans les conditions réelles d'une urgence sanitaire. Coordination, investigation, prise en charge et engagement communautaire : chaque étape de l'intervention est mise à l'épreuve.

Cette montée en puissance en agilité et rapidité intervient alors que la province reste confrontée à une situation préoccupante. Au 25 octobre, plus de 2 309 cas confirmés et 1 293 décès (létalité : 56%) ont été enregistrés au Nord-Kivu. Après plusieurs semaines de ralentissement, une recrudescence des cas est observée, alimentée notamment par des cas importés le long du corridor (Nord-Sud). Les zones de santé de Beni, Katwa, Butembo et Alimbongo demeurent particulièrement exposées.

Le Dr John Otshudiema, Coordonnateur de la riposte de l'OMS au Nord-Kivu, rappelle que la réponse ne repose pas uniquement sur les ressources médicales.

« La confiance est aussi importante que les médicaments. En dotant le Nord-Kivu de deux équipes d’intervention rapide supplémentaires, nous renforçons notre capacité à agir rapidement auprès des communautés qui en ont le plus besoin. »

Car au-delà de l'expertise technique, ces équipes auront également pour mission de renforcer le dialogue avec les populations.

« La formation, la simulation et la certification ne sont pas de simples exercices académiques », souligne la Dre Catherine Smallwood, Gestionnaire de l'incident de la réponse à l’épidémie de la maladie à virus Bundibugyo pour l'OMS en République démocratique du Congo. « Elles garantissent que les équipes déployées pourront fournir une réponse rapide, coordonnée et de qualité lorsque chaque minute compte. »

Sur le terrain, les nouveaux intervenants seront appelés à écouter autant qu'à agir. Informer, répondre aux inquiétudes, accompagner les familles et faciliter l'accès aux soins constituent des composantes essentielles de la riposte.

Guy Mwaka, infirmier formé au cours de cette session, voit dans cette mission une occasion de rétablir durablement la confiance entre les communautés et les services de santé. « Nous voulons que les communautés nous accueillent avec confiance et qu'elles n'aient plus peur de se faire soigner. »

Au-delà de la réponse immédiate à l'épidémie, cet effort contribue à rendre durablement robustes les capacités nationales de préparation et de réponse aux urgences sanitaires, mené par les autorités sanitaires avec l'appui de plusieurs partenaires, dont l'OMS, l'UNICEF, l'UNFPA, OCHA, Africa CDC et International Medical Corps.

Pour le Dr Justus Nsio, Gestionnaire de l'incident pour Africa CDC en RDC, l'héritage le plus durable de cette initiative ne se mesurera pas seulement en vies sauvées aujourd'hui, mais dans la capacité de la RDC à faire face aux crises sanitaires de demain avec ses propres expertises et ressources.

Alors que la lutte contre l’épidémie se poursuit au Nord-Kivu et dans d’autres provinces touchées, ces nouvelles équipes représentent davantage qu'un renfort opérationnel. Elles incarnent un investissement dans les compétences locales, la préparation aux urgences sanitaires et la confiance entre les communautés et le système de santé.

Dans la réponse au virus Bundibugyo, l'accès rapide aux soins sauve des vies. Mais sur le terrain, la confiance reste souvent le premier pas vers la guérison.

fields.title: Providing mental health support to Ebola disease patients and their loved ones
fields.body:
In Butembo, in eastern [Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)](https://www.msf.org/democratic-republic-congo-drc), Kasoki Zawadi spends her days with her husband, who is being treated for [Ebola disease](https://www.msf.org/ebola). A plexiglass window separates them, but they can talk to each other. In Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) treatment centres, [psychological support](https://www.msf.org/mental-health) is available to both patients and their loved ones.

In the corridor of Kitatumba's Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, North Kivu province, Kasoki Zawadi sits on a plastic chair facing the window that separates her from her husband, Victoire. He has been in hospital for 13 days. On the other side of the plastic screen, he smiles from time to time.

The hospital where Victoire is being treated is one of the facilities where MSF supports treatment for patients with Ebola disease. In Butembo, 1,472 cases were confirmed and 735 deaths recorded between May and 22 October 2026.

The outbreak is hitting people already facing insecurity and economic hardship. Many families are sheltering relatives displaced by fighting in neighbouring areas, while movement restrictions and reduced trade have made daily life even harder.

At the treatment centre, teams provide support not only to patients but also their loved ones, as they cope with fear, uncertainty, and the wait for test results. From the moment of admission, psychologists are there to listen to concerns, explain the care being provided, and help families manage the mental strain of hospitalisation.

Every morning, Kasoki arrives at around 6.30 am and stays until 6.30 pm. Her brother-in-law takes over at night.

“We manage to communicate despite the window,” she says. “We’re allowed to see each other, and this brings us comfort.”

> **We manage to communicate despite the window. We’re allowed to see each other, and this brings us comfort.**
> 
> Kasoki Zawadi, whose husband is receiving treatment for Ebola disease

Since her husband was admitted, she has stopped working as a teacher. Their family is supporting them during this time. She also worries about her own health. And when she leaves the centre, the separation weighs heavily on her.

“In the evening, when I go home and can’t see my husband, I find it hard to sleep,” says Kasoki.

A few days later, Kasoki explains that a negative test result had given them hope that they would soon be able to go home. But a second test came back positive.

“When he tested positive again, we were exhausted, mentally and physically,” she says. “Fortunately, the psychologists’ support helped us feel calmer, and we managed to wait.”

## Staying in touch during hospitalisation

The disease and hospitalisation can be distressing for both patients and their loved ones. In Butembo, Patrice Muyisa Kokotz, mental health activity supervisor, provides psychological support. He describes people who arrive not only fearing the disease, but also worried about what awaits them at the centre. Some fear that isolation means they will be abandoned.

> Patrice Muyisa Kokotz, mental health activity supervisor
> 
> **“We give them time to express themselves, talk about their past and their emotions.”**

“We give them time to express themselves, talk about their past and their emotions,” explains Patrice. His team introduces people to how the centre works, explains the care provided, and organises visits. He says seeing other patients and their caregivers helps reassure families.

Some suggest that psychological support can have an impact on patient outcomes.

“Ebola disease is traumatic and sudden; it is a viral illness. So you are under stress, always expecting death at any moment,” says Rachel Kashimoto, a clinical psychologist working with MSF in Beni, also in North Kivu.

“If you are not mentally stable and not well cared for, even physically, things may not go well,” says Rachel. “But if you are mentally stable, well supported, and well monitored, there will also be physical improvement. Because when you have hope of recovering, you follow all the instructions the medical staff give you, and then there can be rapid improvement.”

## Supporting the return home

Psychological support does not end when patients leave the centre. In Mongbwalu, Ituri province, it continues through the survivors’ clinic.

“We organise individual consultations as well as group discussions,” explains Phoebe Zueya Yonkeu, who manages mental health activities at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in Mongbwalu.

“Many tell us they faced stigma when they returned home, lost their jobs or were rejected by their communities, who believed they were still contagious,” says Phoebe. “Others feel guilty towards loved ones who did not survive the disease, and they even wonder whether they were the ones who infected them.”

While some patients face stigma and the trauma of having come close to death after leaving the treatment centre, returning home can also bring immense relief to them and their loved ones.

In Butembo, on the twenty-third day of Victoire’s hospitalisation, the couple learns that he is due to leave that same day. The positive result, following the first negative result, prolonged their wait: now that he has finally tested negative twice.

Kasoki and Victoire say they are very happy to finally be going home.

“Kasoki’s presence really is part of my care,” says Victoire. “I feel comforted. When I see her, it reduces my stress.”

fields.title: Ebola: 10,000 confirmed cases demands rapid scale-up | NRC
fields.body:
NRC is supporting affected communities in areas of Ituri Province, including with the provision of infection prevention and control kits which help fight the spread of Ebola. Photo: NRC

## Ebola: 10,000 confirmed cases demands rapid scale-up

Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) calls for urgent scale-up as outbreak continues to outstrip humanitarian operation

Press release

[DR Congo](https://reliefweb.int/themes?categoryId=47) Published 28. Oct 2026

The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) has now confirmed more than 10,000 cases of Ebola in the current Bundibugyo virus outbreak. The outbreak has affected eight provinces in DR Congo, placing an enormous burden on affected communities. The epidemic is currently concentrated in eastern parts of the country, but recent cases in Kenya and Nigeria have raised fears of a regional flare-up. Almost five thousand deaths have now been confirmed in DR Congo alone.

The outbreak comes on the backdrop of a chronic and neglected humanitarian crisis in eastern DR Congo. NRC has been operational in the country for over two decades, and is taking part in the Ebola response, including in the most affected province of Ituri. NRC urgently calls for sustained and coordinated efforts to protect communities, strengthen access to essential services, and address the needs of people affected by the outbreak and displacement.

“As I move around Ituri I’m seeing just how hard the disease is hitting communities, and I'm struck by how much more needs to be done to bring this outbreak under control,” said Silvia Beccacece, NRC emergency team leader. “Families here have been struggling for years as a result of extreme violence, forced displacement, and the lack of essential services. Ebola comes on top of that, at a point where many have exhausted their ability to cope with the additional challenge it brings. The fact remains that this response is in no way proportionate to the vast scale of the outbreak.”

Combating Ebola requires close cooperation between health authorities, humanitarian organisations, community-based organisations, and international partners. It is essential that the response is scaled up in a way that keeps communities at the centre and is grounded in local customs and traditions. NRC calls on donors and partners to increase their support for humanitarian operations in the DR Congo, particularly in areas affected by the outbreak and displacement.

“10,000 confirmed cases must be a wake-up call that this response is not getting ahead of the outbreak, and is not supporting communities with what they need to bring transmission under control. The warning signs are here for all to see: now it depends on whether leaders will take notice and take the required action,” said Beccacece.

**Note to editors:**

- The latest figure for confirmed Ebola cases in DR Congo is 10,060, with a mortality rate of almost 50 per cent ([National Public Health Institute](https://insp.cd/sitrep-n164-mve-bdbv-25-10-2026/)). The outbreak is now the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history
- NRC operates in 19 affected health zones, with a targeted Ebola response in Ituri, and continues to scale- up its Ebola response while maintaining essential humanitarian assistance in affected and high-risk areas.
- NRC is contributing through an integrated approach combining infection, prevention and control measures, water and sanitation response (WASH), and risk communication and community engagement activities, with a major focus on schools, to make sure they can operate safely. ([NRC](https://reliefweb.int/news/2026/dr-congo-ebola-jeopardising-education-for-100000s-of-children))
- DR Congo has featured on NRC’s neglected displacement crises list for ten consecutive years ([NRC](https://reliefweb.int/news/2026/dr-congo-on-worlds-most-neglected-displacement-crises-list-for-tenth-consecutive-year)).

fields.title: RDC – Nord-Kivu : Couverture des interventions en santé mentale et soutien psychosocial dans la réponse à Ebola, au 21 octobre 2026
fields.body:
Au 21 octobre 2026, onze partenaires assurent des interventions en santé mentale et soutien psychosocial (SMSPS) dans le contexte de la réponse à Ebola au Nord-Kivu. Ils couvrent 77 aires de santé dans 16 des 34 zones de santé, soit 47 %.

Parmi les 17 zones ayant notifié des cas, quatre restent sans couverture SMSPS : Kayna, Alimbongo, Masereka et Musienene. Sept autres zones ont perdu leur couverture après la clôture de projets.

La continuité des services demeure fragile : dix zones dépendent d’un seul partenaire, dont neuf d’ACOPE seule. Dix zones sont couvertes uniquement grâce à des fonds propres. Aucune activité spécifique aux enfants séparés et aux orphelins n’est rapportée.

Les priorités sont de déployer des équipes dans les zones touchées sans couverture, mobiliser des financements dédiés, assurer la relève des projets clôturés et renforcer la coordination avec la Protection de l’enfance. Une actualisation des données est nécessaire pour confirmer la couverture.

fields.title: République démocratique du Congo : Évaluation rapide intégrée en santé publique, Zone de santé de Kasongo Province du Maniema (Juillet 2026)
fields.body:
**PRINCIPALES CONCLUSIONS**

La situation sanitaire et nutritionnelle dans les localités de la Zone de Santé (ZS) de Kasongo affectées (Makiringi 2, Tulombwe 1, Centre Commerciale, Kihogo 1, Ntala et Kitefu) par le choléra et la rougeole dans la province du Maniema demeurait préoccupante, marquée par une surmortalité importante chez les enfants de moins de cinq ans estimée à 6,32 décès pour 10 000 enfants par jour, (IC à 95 % : 2,20-10,45,) et le taux brut de mortalité estimé à 2,11 décès pour 10 000 personnes par jour (IC à 95% : 0,96-3,26). Notre étude a permis de relever qu’il y a un lien étroit entre les problèmes d’accès à l’eau potable, la survenue des flambées de choléra dans une zone de santé endémique de cette maladie, et les cas de malnutrition aiguë sévère chez les enfants. En effet, les difficultés d’accès à l’eau potable et l’inadéquation des services d’hygiène et d’assainissement représentent un facteur important favorisant la transmission du cholera dans la population. Chez les enfants affectés, les épisodes de diarrhées sévères peuvent entrainer ou aggraver la dénutrition en raison de la déshydratation sévère, l’insuffisance des apports alimentaires et la perte de nutriments. L’association du choléra, la malnutrition aiguë sévère et l’inadéquation des services de santé pour faire face à ces urgences exposent les enfants à un risque accru de surmortalité. En effet, cette situation est moins liée à un déficit de consommation alimentaire car les ménages avaient un score de consommation alimentaire acceptable estimé à 92% et 85% des ménages n’avaient expérimenté aucune faim au cours des 4 semaines précédant l’enquête. Cependant, il existait des éléments qui exposent les ménages à un risque d’insécurité alimentaire si des mesures ne sont pas prises. Les terres cultivables deviennent de moins en moins fertiles, les cultures sont attaquées par des ravageurs et la maladie des cultures, la dépendance à l’agriculture de subsistance, l’amenuisement des sources de revenus stables des ménages et la fonctionnalité des marchés se détériorant.

Jusqu’à présent, les ménages s’adaptent bien à la détérioration progressive des moyens d’existence. Il s’avère nécessaire de renforcer leur résilience à travers un appui aux moyens d’existence agricoles, incluant la distribution d’intrants agricoles tenant compte du problème de fertilité des sols, l’amélioration de l’accès aux semences et aux outils de production, ainsi que le soutien aux activités génératrices de revenus. Renforcer également les actions visant à améliorer l’accès aux marchés et à diversifier les sources de revenus afin de réduire la dépendance à l’agriculture de subsistance. L’amélioration des indicateurs de santé, passe par une prise en considération ardue des problèmes d’accès à l’eau potable, la vaccination de masse incluant les vaccins contre le cholera et la rougeole et le renforcement des capacités des formations sanitaires.

fields.body:

**Synopsis (short abstract)** The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), through Data in Emergencies (DIEM), conducted a qualitative study of the impact of Ebola disease and conflict on agricultural livelihoods in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu provinces in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This rapid assessment used a cross-sectional, mixed-methods design based on semi-structured key informant interviews conducted in August 2026 across the three provinces. The assessment is the first stage in a larger study that will integrate quantitative household survey data in the coming months.

fields.body:
**Niger**  
*Un incendie touche près de 100 ménages déplacés dans la région de Diffa*

Le 21 octobre, un incendie s'est déclaré dans un site de déplacés internes à N'Guigmi, dans l'est de la région de Diffa, affectant environ 100 ménages, selon les rapports préliminaires. L’incident a exacerbé la vulnérabilité des familles déplacées déjà confrontées à des conditions de vie précaires. Dans un contexte de baisse du financement humanitaire et d’arrivée de températures plus froides, les ménages touchés sont confrontés à des risques accrus en matière de protection, de sécurité alimentaire et de santé. Une aide urgente est nécessaire pour répondre aux besoins immédiats et empêcher une nouvelle détérioration des conditions de vie.

**Congo**  
*Les inondations touchent près de 43 000 personnes dans le nord de la Likouala*

Le gouvernement a lancé une réponse d'urgence pour venir en aide à près de 43 000 personnes touchées par de graves inondations dans le département de la Likouala, dans le nord de la République du Congo. Les eaux de crue ont submergé des villages, endommagé des infrastructures et déplacé des milliers de personnes. Les autorités ont établi un pont aérien pour acheminer de la nourriture, des médicaments et des fournitures d'urgence, complété par un transport fluvial. Des plans sont également en cours pour relocaliser les familles touchées et intensifier l’aide humanitaire.

**République démocratique du Congo**  
*La violence contre les agents de santé menace la réponse à Ebola*

Le coordonnateur principal d'Ebola, Julien Harneis, a condamné le meurtre d'une infirmière impliquée dans la réponse à Ebola à Bafwasende, dans la province de la Tshopo, le 24 octobre. L'agent de santé aurait été attaqué par des manifestants, tandis qu'un directeur d'école soutenant la riposte aurait été grièvement blessé. Par ailleurs, un centre de santé à Kisangani a été pillé, des fournitures médicales ont été volées et un agent de santé a été agressé et temporairement détenu. Ces incidents soulignent les inquiétudes croissantes concernant la violence et la méfiance qui minent la réponse à Ebola, alors que les cas confirmés approchent les 10 000 dans tout le pays. L'ONU s'engage auprès des autorités pour renforcer la protection des agents et des établissements de santé et garantir la fourniture en toute sécurité des services essentiels.

*L’épidémie de choléra s’aggrave en raison de graves lacunes en matière d’approvisionnement en eau et d’assainissement*

Plus de 55 000 cas suspects de choléra ont été signalés dans tout le pays depuis janvier, la province du Tanganyika, dans le sud-est de la RDC, étant particulièrement touchée. Toutes les zones de santé de la province ont signalé des cas, avec plus de 6 300 infections enregistrées, soit près de 1 000 de plus qu'au cours de la même période en 2025. À Kalemie, les installations de traitement sont débordées, tandis qu'un accès limité à l'eau potable et à l'assainissement alimente la transmission. Les sites de déplacement accueillant plus de 6 500 personnes ont été touchés, et plus de 12 000 personnes déplacées sont en danger. L'ONU et ses partenaires humanitaires fournissent des traitements, des fournitures médicales et la chloration de l'eau, mais des ressources supplémentaires sont nécessaires de toute urgence pour accroître la capacité de réponse et améliorer l'accès à l'eau potable et à l'assainissement.

fields.title: West and Central Africa: Latest Events at a glance (20–26 October 2026)
fields.body:
**Republic of the Congo**  
*Flooding affects nearly 43,000 people in northern Likouala*

The Government has launched an emergency response to assist nearly 43,000 people affected by severe flooding in Likouala Department, in northern Republic of the Congo. Floodwaters have submerged villages, damaged infrastructure and displaced thousands of people. Authorities have established an air bridge to deliver food, medicines and emergency supplies, complemented by river transport. Plans are also underway to relocate affected families and scale up humanitarian assistance.

**Niger**  
*Fire affects nearly 100 displaced households in Diffa Region*

On 21 October, a fire broke out at an IDP site in N’Guigmi, in eastern Diffa Region, affecting approximately 100 households, according to preliminary reports. The incident has exacerbated the vulnerability of displaced families already facing precarious living conditions. Amid declining humanitarian funding and the onset of colder weather, affected households face heightened protection, food security and health risks. Urgent assistance is needed to address immediate needs and prevent further deterioration of living conditions.

**Democratic Republic of the Congo**  
*Violence against health workers threatens Ebola response*

Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis condemned the killing of a nurse involved in the Ebola response in Bafwasende, Tshopo Province, on 24 October. The health worker was reportedly attacked by protesters, while a school principal supporting the response was seriously injured. Separately, a health centre in Kisangani was looted, with medical supplies stolen and a health worker assaulted and temporarily detained. These incidents underscore growing concerns over violence and mistrust undermining the Ebola response, as confirmed cases approach 10,000 nationwide. The UN is engaging with authorities to strengthen the protection of health workers and facilities and ensure the safe delivery of essential services.

*Cholera outbreak worsens amid critical water and sanitation gaps*

More than 55,000 suspected cholera cases have been reported nationwide since January, with Tanganyika Province, in south-eastern DRC, particularly affected. All health zones in the province have reported cases, with over 6,300 infections recorded, nearly 1,000 more than during the same period in 2025. In Kalemie, treatment facilities are overwhelmed, while limited access to safe water and sanitation is fuelling transmission. Displacement sites hosting over 6,500 people have been affected, with more than 12,000 displaced people at risk. The UN and humanitarian partners are providing treatment, medical supplies and water chlorination, but additional resources are urgently needed to expand response capacity and improve access to safe water and sanitation.

fields.title: DRC’s worst outbreak: 10,000 Ebola cases confirmed as children lose parents, schooling and safety
fields.body:
With some 4,887 deaths since the start of the outbreak, children are becoming sick and dying from the illness, being orphaned, separated from loved ones, and missing critical months of education.

**KINSHASA, 27 October 2026 -** More than [10,000 people](https://ebola-tracker.org/en/data/) have now been infected in the Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) Ebola outbreak, the largest ever recorded in the country's history and the second largest globally, with children paying a devastating price, Save the Children said.

With some [4,887 deaths](https://ebola-tracker.org/en/data/) since the start of the outbreak – and a devastating case fatality rate of 48.6% – children are becoming sick and dying from the illness, being orphaned, separated from loved ones, and missing critical months of education.

In the 2014–2015 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, the worst ever recorded globally, more than [28,600 people were infected](https://www.who.int/emergencies/situations/ebola-outbreak-2014-2016-West-Africa) and 11,325 people died, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). More than [22,000 children](https://reliefweb.int/report/guinea/unicef-welcomes-declaration-end-ebola-outbreak-guinea) also lost one or both of their parents.

This current outbreak, which was declared on 15 May 2026 in Ituri Province in eastern DRC, has spread from a single health zone to 66 health zones across eight provinces and continues to affect communities already facing conflict, displacement, food insecurity and weakened health services.

More than 1,900 children have also been orphaned or separated from one or both parents or caregivers, Save the Children said, with [nearly two children a day,](https://www.savethechildren.net/news/nearly-two-children-day-orphaned-dr-congos-latest-ebola-outbreak-save-children) on average, being orphaned, creating devastating risks for their safety and wellbeing.

There is currently no approved vaccine specifically for the Bundibugyo Ebola strain driving the outbreak, making prevention, surveillance, community engagement and access to healthcare critical to slowing transmission, said Save the Children.

More than 2,700 children have been infected since the outbreak began and hundreds have lost their lives, according to the Africa CDC and WHO. Young children remain particularly vulnerable, with [children under five facing](https://www.savethechildren.org/us/about-us/media-and-news/2026-press-releases/DRC-ebola-outbreak-killed-one-thousand-children) significantly higher mortality rates than the overall outbreak average, with a case fatality rate of 72% \[1\].

**Greg Ramm, Save the Children Country Director in the DRC, said:**

"The confirmation of more than 10,000 Ebola cases is a stark reminder of the scale of this crisis and the urgent need to strengthen the response before even more lives are lost. Behind this milestone are thousands of families facing unimaginable fear and uncertainty, and children are bearing some of the heaviest consequences.

"This outbreak is unfolding in communities already affected by conflict, displacement and food insecurity. Families are struggling to access healthcare, health facilities are under immense pressure, and many communities lack the resources needed to prevent transmission and keep children safe.

"For children, the risks extend far beyond infection. We are seeing children lose parents and caregivers, miss out on healthcare and education, and face increased protection risks as families' coping mechanisms are stretched to breaking point. The longer this outbreak continues, the greater the impact will be on children's health, wellbeing and futures.

"The absence of a vaccine specifically approved for this strain means there is no room for complacency. We urgently need increased investment in disease surveillance, infection prevention and control, safe isolation and care, community engagement, and support for frontline health workers. At the same time, essential services such as healthcare, nutrition, education and child protection must remain available, so children do not suffer the wider consequences of the outbreak.

"Containing this outbreak remains possible, but it requires rapid, coordinated action. The international community must not look away. Every delay gives the virus further opportunities to spread and places more children at risk."

Save the Children has been responding since the outbreak was first declared in May and has reached nearly 200,000 people, including more than 100,000 children, through Ebola preparedness and response activities in Ituri Province. The organisation is supporting infection prevention and control in health facilities, community awareness and risk communication activities, case detection and referral, and the continuity of essential health, nutrition, education and child protection services.

The child rights organisation is also establishing Observation Care Centres for children who have been exposed to Ebola and cannot safely remain with family members during the observation period. The first centre in Bunia, the capital of Ituri Province, is expected to open this month and will provide accommodation, health monitoring, nutrition support, psychosocial care, learning and recreational activities for children.

ENDS

NOTES:

\[1\] According to the Continental Incident Management Support Team Joint WHO & Africa CDC Response, 26 October 2026: 2,705 aged 0-17 are among the confirmed cases, of which 1345 are children under 5; CFR among children under 5 is 72%.

fields.title: COI Query Response - DRC: Situation of women without a support network in Kinshasa and South Kivu
fields.body:
**1. Background information**

Throughout 2025, the security, humanitarian and human rights situation in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continued to deteriorate. Escalating violence involving the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), an armed group linked to the Islamic State, and renewed confrontations between the Rwandan-backed M23 movement and government forces had a severe impact on the civilian population. 1 The provinces of North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri were particularly affected, with the conflict resulting in increasing civilian casualties and largescale displacement. Human Rights Watch (HRW) also reported numerous abuses by armed groups, including conflict-related sexual violence.2 According to UN women, women and girls were ‘disproportionately’ affected.3 In June 2026, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reported Ebola cases in South Kivu and noted challenges related to surveillance and testing. According to MSF, communities in the province have long faced ‘chronic gaps in healthcare and a limited humanitarian response’, which have hindered efforts to control the outbreak.4 This query is an update of two previously published EUAA queries: Situation of women without a support network in South Kivu, published on 2 September 2024, and Situation of women without a support network in Kinshasa, published on 25 August 2023. Additionally, information on gender-based violence against women in the DRC can be found in the EUAA query, Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) against women, published in June 2025. Information on the situation of women who have children out of wedlock can be found in the EUAA query, Situation of women who have children out of wedlock, including legal framework, treatment by society, and access to support services, published in February 2024.

fields.title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 30 September
fields.body:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- Children continued to bear a disproportionate share of the outbreak. As of 30 September, children accounted for approximately 27 per cent of confirmed cases but nearly 38 per cent of deaths, with children under five representing almost two-thirds of child deaths.
- In response to the outbreak’s geographic expansion, UNICEF scaled up its multisectoral operations from 60 to 63 health zones, maintaining a presence in all 16 hotspots.
- Community-based surveillance was strengthened through the deployment of 3,469 additional community mobilizers. Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) activities expanded to 55 affected health zones, mobilizing 11,513 frontline and community actors, extending collaboration from 108 to 114 radio stations, and launching intensified digital engagement and rumour management.
- Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) interventions transitioned from initial deployment to implementation at scale. UNICEF delivered more than 590,000 litres of safe water, expanded support to health facilities and schools, strengthened decontamination capacity, and deployed assistance to newly affected areas.
- With the start of the school year, 167,343 children and adolescents accessed safe and adapted learning opportunities, while 158,188 unique children received school or IPC/WASH kits.
- UNICEF requires US$ 113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan. As of 30 September, US$ 41 million had been mobilized, leaving a US$ 72.5 million funding gap. Timely, flexible funding is urgently required to sustain outbreak control, protect children and maintain essential health including mental health and psychosocial support, nutrition, education, IPC/WASH and protection services in communities already affected by conflict, displacement and cholera.

**EPIDEMIOLOGICAL SITUATION UPDATE**

Between 1 and 30 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 2,050 additional confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases and 979 deaths. As of 30 September, cumulative confirmed cases had reached 8,300, including 4,018 deaths, corresponding to a case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.4 per cent. The outbreak continued to expand geographically, with confirmed cases reported for the first time in Sud-Ubangi Province, bringing the number of affected provinces to seven (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé and South-Ubangi).

During September, an additional three health zones reported confirmed cases, increasing the total to 63 affected health zones, representing 37.7 per cent of the country's 167 health zones. 16 health zones across North Kivu, Ituri and Haut-Uélé provinces were identified as Ebola hotspots, highlighting the scale of transmission and the need for increased prevention, surveillance and response measures. UNICEF maintained an operational presence across all 16 hotspot health zones, delivering services in support of the Ebola response.

The outbreak is now the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. Ituri province remains the epicentre, accounting for 75.8 per cent of all confirmed cases 6,293 cases and 2,902 deaths, followed by North Kivu 1,601 cases and 950 deaths and Haut-Uélé 346 cases and 144 deaths. Transmission also continued in Tshopo, Bas-Uélé, South Kivu and South-Ubangi. Women and girls represent approximately 53.4 per cent of reported confirmed cases.

Children aged 17 years and below account for approximately 27.4 per cent of confirmed cases and 37.6 per cent of reported deaths, indicating a disproportionate mortality burden among children. Children under five bear the greatest burden, representing approximately 63.8 per cent of deaths among children aged 17 years and below.

During September, 16 health workers were identified among confirmed cases reported during the month, underscoring ongoing risks to frontline responders.

fields.title: Ebola response: Disinformation kills, care saves lives
fields.body:
**Bunia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo—**“They said that at the hospital, they would give my child bad injections and he would die,” says Jeanne\*, her voice trembling. These words deeply marked this mother whose six year old child showed suspected symptoms of Ebola. Out of fear of treatment centres, she first sought solutions elsewhere. When her child was finally taken to a health facility, his condition was already critical. Forty eight hours later, he died.

Today, Jeanne shares her testimony to prevent other families from experiencing the same tragedy.

It all began with a fever and vomiting. Thinking it was malaria, she opted for self medication. But her child’s condition did not improve. Around her, disinformation portrayed Ebola as a commercial scheme and claimed that patients received lethal injections in treatment centres. These falsehoods fueled her mistrust.

She then consulted a traditional healer her family had relied on before. “I took my son to our healer. I had hope because he had treated our family for a long time,” Jeanne explains.

The child gradually weakened. As his condition worsened, the healer recommended transfer to a health facility. “It was truly painful to lose my child. I deeply regret not going quickly to the health centre,” says the grieving mother.

Her testimony reveals how disinformation can influence decisions about seeking appropriate care.

For Salif Diarra, social listening analyst at the World Health Organization (WHO), this story should not be seen as an individual fault. “This mother wanted to protect her child. But rumours fueled fear that influenced her decision. When a family sees the treatment centre as a threat, they may hesitate to seek help, even as their loved one’s condition deteriorates,” he says.

Such accounts are not isolated. Social listening teams regularly identify claims about supposed lethal injections and rumours that undermine trust in public health interventions.

To address this, WHO supports health authorities in analysing community concerns through media, social networks and the toll free number 151.

Between May and September 2026, more than 34 650 items of online content were analysed, including rumours and concerns.

Three times a week, Ministry of Health and WHO teams review information gathered from communities to identify mis- and disinformation that could delay care seeking. According to Diarra, these exchanges help adapt messages and interventions to community concerns, strengthening trust in the Ebola response.

In Rwampara health zone, demystification sessions were organized to address fears about treatment centres. WHO, with partner support, also helped train 100 traditional healers, 20 social media influencers and 150 hotline operators to improve access to reliable information.

In Ituri, these efforts include community dialogues and public forums. Frédérick Mungobijira, head of infodemic management in Ituri, recalls a situation in Katogu health area where rumours had sparked strong resistance to response teams. “We organized community dialogues with local leaders to explain the disease and fight misinformation. After these exchanges, response teams were able to access communities that had previously been hostile.”

Since the start of the outbreak, more than 1000 rumours have been addressed in Ituri. These interventions help reduce resistance and encourage early care seeking.

For Jeanne, healing also requires psychological support. After her child’s death, she attends sessions with a WHO psychologist who helps her express her grief and gradually regain emotional balance. “The psychologist helps me a lot. He listens, advises and supports me. Today, I feel better,” she says.

Jeanne’s sister denounces the influence of rumours, disinformation and misinformation. “Some people said it was dangerous to take a sick person to the hospital, that they might never return alive. Today, we stay close to our sister, listen to her and encourage her to overcome this ordeal. We are all deeply affected. The little one was full of life,” she says.

For Diarra, restoring trust requires listening to communities and responding concretely to their concerns. “Reliable information must be accessible, understandable and delivered by people communities trust. We must listen to families’ fears and respond with respect,” he says.

Despite her grief, Jeanne has chosen to testify to encourage other parents to seek care quickly. “I ask all parents not to believe mis- and disinformation. As soon as a child is sick, you must go quickly to a health centre to receive appropriate care. I would not want another mother to live what I have lived,” she says.

fields.title: Ebola survivor clinics strengthen the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
fields.body:
**Bunia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo—** Leaving an Ebola treatment centre (ETC) does not mark the end of a patient’s care journey. In Bunia, the capital of Ituri Province, the survivor clinic takes over from treatment centres to support survivors through to the completion of their physical and psychological recovery. Beyond medical care, these clinics provide spaces for listening, support and assistance with social reintegration.

“We cannot have a successful response without a survivor clinic,” says Dr Huguette Mbuyi Musadi, a member of the Ministry of Health’s survivor identification and follow-up pillar. For her, medical recovery alone is not enough. Since the beginning of the outbreak, more than 2700 people have been declared cured and require post-recovery medical follow-up. “When a survivor comes to the clinic, we examine them from head to toe to check whether they have any disorders or associated conditions, such as diabetes or hypertension. Above all, however, we must manage the aftereffects linked to Ebola,” she says.

The effects of Ebola can take different forms, including joint pain, chronic fatigue, neurological disorders, particularly memory difficulties, as well as psychological manifestations such as stress and irritability. “As a survivor, I can say that forgetfulness is common. You may forget something today and only remember it two days later. Then there is irritability and a great deal of stress,” says Ganisikalé, an Ebola survivor.

To manage Ebola-related conditions even after recovery, the Ministry of Health, in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO) and with support from UN’s Central Emergency Fund and the UK government, established its first survivor clinic in Bunia, the epicentre of the outbreak. Operational since 19 September 2026, the clinic had provided care to more than 400 Ebola survivors. A second survivor clinic was established in Beni, North Kivu Province and has been receiving survivors since 17 October 2026.

Beyond health services, the clinics provide an environment where survivors can speak openly about their challenges and receive support to overcome stigma within their communities. These medical facilities are a natural continuation of the care provided by ETCs.

“Once patients leave the ETC, they may experience physical as well as psychological complications and we are here to provide comprehensive care,” says Dr Roland Kasamaga, Coordinator of the Bunia Survivor Clinic. “Without these clinics, the consequences could be severe. The aftereffects can impact a person throughout their life. It is important for survivors to continue receiving care so that their health and well-being can be restored comprehensively and over the long term.”

Another crucial role of the clinics is biological surveillance. The Ebola virus can persist in certain bodily fluids, particularly semen, for months after recovery. If survivors are not monitored, there could be a resurgence of the disease or a relapse.

A survivor’s care at the clinic includes consultations in general medicine, psychology and nutrition, as well as laboratory tests. The process takes an average of two hours. At the pharmacy, the final stage of the care process, nurse Elisée Mbusi emphasizes the importance of taking medication correctly and adopting preventive measures. “We provide condoms to men because studies have shown that the virus can remain in semen for a long time. If a survivor continues to engage in unprotected sexual activity, they expose their partner to risk,” she says.

For WHO, survivor clinics serve two key objectives. “First, they help prevent the resurgence of the disease within the community from people who have already recovered. Second, they address the physical, psychological and nutritional conditions experienced by survivors and provide holistic support that meets their needs,” explains Dr Brys Busanga, WHO focal person for survivor follow-up. “Without survivor follow-up, the response is incomplete. That is why WHO integrates this component into the response, so that the package of interventions is complete.”

Beyond healthcare, survivor clinics also play a community mobilization role. Aimée, a survivor who has become a community mobilizer, explains how she encourages survivors to attend the clinic. “We have a list of survivors and we call them to inform them about the clinic and invite them to come for follow-up consultations. We also tell them that transport costs will be reimbursed,” she explains. The strategy is proving successful. More than 90% of the survivors who are contacted attend their follow-up appointments.

Christian Buna, an Ebola survivor, was contacted by Aimée and visited the clinic two days later. “I was declared cured several months ago. I came for a follow-up check-up. I was told that everything is fine, but that I should continue with follow-up care,” he says. “I was listened to and reassured. I am truly satisfied with the work of the health workers. This clinic is extremely important.”

Christian has committed himself to mobilizing other survivors to attend regular follow-up consultations. “I will encourage others to come for their check-ups because it is important to understand and monitor your physical and mental condition after such an ordeal,” he says.

The Ebola response does not end at the doors of ETCs. Survivor follow-up clinics extend these efforts by ensuring biological surveillance, managing long-term health effects, combating stigma and strengthening community mobilization. They serve as a reminder that recovery is not only a medical victory, but also a process of human and social reconstruction. In these spaces, survivors become active participants in the response, bearers of hope and living proof that resilience is possible in the face of Ebola.

The clinics embody a new dimension of the response. “When you go to another hospital, you feel ashamed to say that you are an Ebola survivor. Here, we are free to talk about anything and everything,” says Ganisikalé. “In our clinic, I feel comfortable. It really helps us.”
